newsitem.title: USA: Fed hike fails to spell relief for corp bond mart.
newsitem.headline: Fed hike fails to spell relief for corp bond mart.

text.p: Corporate bond players sat out Tuesday's session as a widely expected hike in interest rates by the U.S. Federal Reserve Board failed to provide a sense of relief, which spurred new fears in the marketplace, traders said.
"There's a feeling of hesitation out there following the Fed tightening," said one trader. "New fears that this may be the first of several to come have filled the market."
On Tuesday, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy-setting arm of the Fed, voted to hike the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
No change was made in the Federal Reserve discount rate, which remains at 5.0 percent.
Fears that the Fed may be at the beginning of a new tightening cycle filled the market amid a volatile U.S. Treasury market, players said.

"People were kind of expecting some sort of relief rally in the (Treasury) market following the Fed tightening, which in turn was expected to help ours...it turned out to be a very brief one," another trader said.
After the Fed's annoucement, U.S. Treasuries turned briefly higher only to quickly erase gains. The U.S. T-bond closed off 17/32 at 95-23/32 to yield 6.97 percent.
"The market traded up a little bit then shortly after sold off a 1/2 point," said another trader. "There hasn't been much movement since then...people just seem to be sitting on what they have."
Players said market activity which was next to nil before the Fed's move remained quiet, although some buying activity was seen shortly after the Fed's announcement.
The Fed tightening which was aimed at tempering U.S. economic growth could mark the beginning of the end for historically tight corporate bond spreads, market players said.

"If this is the first move designed to slow down the economy, this will start to put doubt into people's minds about corporate bonds," said Peter Hegel, chief investment officer for fixed income at Van Kampen American Capital.
"This probably gets the process of widening spreads going," said Hegel, who oversees $26 billion in assets.

Hegel said spreads in the overall corporate bond market could widen gradually by 10 to 20 basis points over the rest of the year, assuming the Fed raises interest rates at least one more time as he expects.
Meanwhile, the high-yield sector saw very little activity with prices ending unchanged to down 1/4, traders said.
"We haven't really seen many buyers in the market but things still haven't really cheapened up yet," said one high-yield trader.
"If things do cheapen up I'm sure we'll see some buying on the break," he added.
Earlier in the day, some trading activity was seen in the cable and broadcasting sector, but players said activity later leveled off.
In the primary sector, two new deals stirred up some action in an otherwise quiet market, traders said.
Qwest Communications International sold $250 million in 10-7/8 percent 10-year notes to yield 412.5 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. Salomon Brothers was lead manager on the deal.

In addition, TravelCenters of America Inc issued $125 million in 10-1/4 percent 10-year 144A notes to yield 355 basis point over Treasuries. The deal was underwritten by Chase Securities Inc, sources said.
